title: Water to the west
hookLine: at Hardwar, seeing pilgrims throw water toward the rising sun, he throws his westward, to water his fields

lines: THE ROAST, AND THE SMALL PAN.
HARDWAR, ON THE GANGES, AT DAWN.
cards: The old joke goes like this. A woman always cut the end off the roast before she cooked it. Her daughter asked why.
Because my mother did. So they asked the grandmother, who said: my pan was too small. A habit can outlive its reason.
Now, a riverbank at dawn. Hardwar, a pilgrimage town where the Ganges comes down out of the mountains. Crowds stand in the cold river at sunrise.
And a stranger from the Punjab wades in among them and does something that makes everyone stop and stare.

teach.b: The pilgrims were cupping water in their hands and throwing it toward the rising sun, in the east. Tradition says it was an offering, meant to reach their ancestors in the next world.
Nanak turned his back to the sun and threw water the other way, west. People gathered. What are you doing?
Watering my fields back home in the Punjab, he answered, as the story goes. They laughed. Your fields are far away.

teach.h: IF YOURS REACHES THEM, WHY NOT MINE?
teach.b: How can water thrown here reach them? And there's the turn. If your water can reach your ancestors in another world, he asked, why can't mine reach my fields in the Punjab?
It's a funny story, and it's meant to be. But notice what Nanak isn't doing. He isn't mocking the pilgrims' love for their parents and grandparents.

teach.h: LOOK AT THE ACT, NOT JUST THE HABIT.
teach.b: He's asking them to look at the act.
Why do we do this? Does the water go where we think it goes? What would actually help?
That question runs right through his hymns: washing the body at holy places doesn't wash the mind, and what God looks at is the heart and the way a person lives.

To say it carefully: for the Hindus at Hardwar, then and now, bathing in the Ganges carries deep meaning, and this story is told by Sikhs about their Guru. It's his question, not a verdict on anyone's grandmother.
And the question travels. Any family, any office can have water it throws east without asking why.

how: Sikhs tell the Hardwar sakhi as a teaching that outward ritual without inner meaning does not reach God; a gurdwara at Hardwar marks the place tradition links to the story.

his hymns often say bathing the body doesn't wash the mind

games.q: you're on the Ganges at dawn. the whole crowd is throwing water east, toward the sun. what do you do?
o: join in, and throw it east.
turn around and throw it west.
stand on the bank and lecture them.
games.why: Nanak threw his water west, toward his fields. when they laughed, he asked: if yours reaches the next world, why can't mine reach the Punjab?

practice: Pick something you do every day without thinking: the route you drive, the way you start a meeting, something you always say. Ask it kindly, the way you'd ask a child: why do we do this?
Maybe there's a great reason and you'll keep it gladly; maybe the pan was just too small, and either way, you'll know.

wordCard.voice: Hardwar. The pilgrimage town on the Ganges where Guru Nanak threw water west, toward his fields, to ask what an offering actually does.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jal, water; a word shared across Punjabi, Hindi and Sanskrit.
